tip: 안 (an = not) goes right before the verb, no helper needed: 안 먹었어요 (an meogeosseoyo) = didn't eat. Korean has no "do" for negatives.
Questions don't rearrange anything – 저녁 먹었어요? (jeonyeok meogeosseoyo) is the exact statement with rising tone. No "did you" flip.
Two subjects, no problem: 이 식당은 (i sikdang-eun) sets the topic, 불고기가 (bulgogi-ga) is the subject – "as for this place, the bulgogi is famous."
을/를 (eul/reul) tags the object: 한국 음식을 (hanguk eumsigeul = Korean food). Once tagged it can move around the sentence – the verb just stays last.
있어요 (isseoyo) covers both "there is" and "have": 자리 있어요? (jari isseoyo) is literally "does a seat exist?" – no separate verb for "have."
인분 (inbun = serving) takes Sino numbers: 2인분 reads 이인분 (i-inbun), never native 두 (du). Each counter picks its own number system.
Korean flips "a bottle of soju": the drink comes first, then number + counter – 소주 한 병 (soju han byeong = soju one bottle).
One letter apart: 달라요 (dallayo) = different, 달아요 (darayo) = sweet. 맛이 조금 달라요 (masi jogeum dallayo) = the taste is a bit different, not a bit sweet.
Korean has no verb "to need" – 필요 없어요 (piryo eopseoyo) is literally "necessity doesn't exist." To need something: 필요해요 (piryohaeyo).
에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 앱에서 (aebeseo = on the app) pairs with 주문했어요 (jumunhaesseoyo = ordered). Plain 에 (e) is just location, no action.
돼요 (dwaeyo) is the all-purpose "it works / it's fine": 카드 돼요 (kadeu dwaeyo) = cards are accepted. Noun + 돼요? asks if anything is possible.
The -ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending is a promise to the listener: 살게요 (salgeyo) = "I'll buy – I've got this." Plain 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) just states a plan.
씨 (ssi) after a name is the polite default – 민수 씨 (Minsu ssi). It follows the given name, and you never attach it to your own.
Double consonant matters: 쌌어요 (ssasseoyo) = was cheap, 샀어요 (sasseoyo) = bought. 싸다 (ssada = cheap) vs 사다 (sada = buy).
